Pontinho is a card game in which players form sets and runs to get rid of the cards in their hands.

A match is played over multiple rounds. When a player has no cards left, they go out and end the round. The other players receive points for the cards still in their hands.

Points accumulate throughout the match. As soon as any player reaches 101 points or more, the match ends.

The player with the lowest accumulated score wins.

Pontinho uses two standard 52-card decks without printed jokers, for a total of 104 cards.

Each player receives nine cards. The remaining cards are placed face down in the center of the table to form the draw pile.

The discard pile, where cards discarded during the round are placed, sits beside the draw pile.

One card is turned face up to determine the wildcards for the round. Every card of the next rank and the same color as the turned card becomes a wildcard.

Because two decks are used, there are four wildcards each round.

For example, if the turned card is 7♥, the four red eights are wildcards: two 8♥ and two 8♦.

Likewise, if the turned card is 5♣, the four black sixes are wildcards: two 6♣ and two 6♠.

Play proceeds counterclockwise.

Cards may be combined into sets or runs.

SETS

A set consists of three cards of the same rank and different suits.

Example: 8♠ 8♥ 8♣

Two cards of the same suit may not be used in the same set, even if they come from different decks.

Sets contain exactly three cards. A fourth card may not be added to a set already on the table.

RUNS

A run consists of three or more consecutive cards of the same suit.

Example: 4♦ 5♦ 6♦ 7♦

An Ace may be used before the 2 or after the King.

Examples:

• A♠ 2♠ 3♠
• Q♥ K♥ A♥

An Ace may not be used to connect the King to the 2 within the same run.

On their turn, a player must draw a card from the draw pile or take the most recently discarded card.

After drawing, they may lay down sets and runs, add cards to melds on the table, and make any other permitted plays.

A completed combination does not have to be laid down immediately. The player may keep it in hand for later use.

To end their turn, the player must discard one card unless they have gone out.

Play continues counterclockwise, subject to the plays that are allowed out of turn.

On their turn, a player may take the top card from the draw pile.

The drawn card becomes part of their hand and may be used immediately or kept for a later play.

After drawing, the player continues normally and may lay down melds, extend combinations, and discard.
6. Taking the discard on your turn

The current player may choose to take the most recently discarded card instead of drawing from the pile.

In this case, the card does not have to be used immediately.

It may be kept in hand and used on a future play.

For example, if the previous player discards 7♠, you may take it even without a completed combination for that card.

Only the most recently discarded card is available. Earlier cards in the discard pile may not be selected.
7. Taking the discard out of turn

A player may also take the most recently discarded card when it is not their turn.

In that case, the card must be used immediately to lay down a valid meld.

A card taken out of turn may not simply be kept in the hand.

EXAMPLE

You hold 5♥ and 6♥. Another player discards 7♥.

Even though it is not your turn, you may take 7♥ and lay down the run 5♥ 6♥ 7♥.

However, if you hold only 5♥, you may not take 7♥ hoping to complete the run later.

Taking the discard out of turn does not require going out. You only need to lay down a valid meld using the card you took.

After the play, normal table order is maintained. The player who would have been next must draw a card from the draw pile and continue their turn normally.

When more than one player wants the same discarded card, priority follows the counterclockwise order of play.

The next player has first choice. If that player does not use the card, the opportunity passes to the others in table order.

EXAMPLE

At a four-player table, the order is:

A → B → C → D → A

If player A discards a card, priority goes to B, then C, and finally D.

Player B may take the card and keep it in hand because it is B’s turn.

Players C and D may take the card only to lay down a meld immediately.

If both want the card, C has priority over D.

Exception: immediately going out using the most recently discarded card takes priority over any ordinary pickup, regardless of player order.

During their turn, a player may lay down any sets and runs they can form.

They do not need to lay down every meld at once. Some combinations may be played while other cards remain in the hand.

Melds remain on the table until the end of the round.

Once laid down, the cards no longer count as cards in hand and are not scored if another player goes out.

Players may add cards to runs already laid down on the table, including their opponents’ runs.

For example, if the run 5♣ 6♣ 7♣ is on the table, a player may add 4♣ or 8♣.

Added cards must keep the combination valid.

Ordinary cards may not be removed from melds already on the table to create new combinations.

Wildcards are defined at the start of each round according to the card turned during setup.

The four cards one rank above the turned card and of the same color are wildcards.

For example, if 7♥ is turned, both 8♥ and both 8♦ are wildcards.

A wildcard may replace a missing card in a run.

For example:

5♦ – Wildcard – 7♦

In this case, the wildcard represents 6♦.

A wildcard must occupy an internal position in a run, between two cards that establish its value.

A wildcard may not be placed at either end of a run or used to form a set.

A wildcard may also be used as an ordinary card according to its printed rank and suit.

Wildcards may never be discarded under any circumstances.

A player holding a wildcard must use it in a valid combination to get rid of it.

A wildcard used in a run may be recovered when another player holds the card that it represents.

To make the exchange, the player must put the real card in the wildcard’s place.

EXAMPLE

The table contains the run:

5♠ – Wildcard – 7♠

A player holding 6♠ may place it in the run and recover the wildcard.

The recovered wildcard must be used immediately in another valid combination.

It may not be removed and kept in the hand or saved for a future play.

The exchange also may not leave the original run invalid.

Discarding normally ends a player’s turn.

After drawing and making their plays, the player chooses one ordinary card from the hand to discard.

A card that could be used in a meld on the table may still be discarded.

The only restriction is that wildcards may never be discarded, even when used according to their printed rank.

The most recently discarded card becomes available to the other players under the pickup and priority rules.

A player goes out when they have no cards left in their hand.

This may happen by laying down new combinations, extending existing melds, or using a discarded card.

A player does not necessarily need to make a final discard to go out. If they use every card in their hand in valid combinations, they may end the round immediately.

As soon as a player goes out, the round ends.

The player who went out receives no points. Every other player scores the cards still in their hand.
15. Going out with the latest discard

If a newly discarded card lets a player empty their hand, they may take it and go out immediately, even out of turn.

This play requires no additional discard and has the highest priority over ordinary pickups.

EXAMPLE

You hold only 2♠ and 3♠.

Another player discards 4♠.

You may take 4♠, lay down the run 2♠ 3♠ 4♠, and go out immediately.

This play takes priority even over the next player, who would normally have first choice to take the discarded card.

The go-out must be made immediately after the discard, before the next play is completed.
16. Going out by extending a newly played meld

A player may also go out when a meld just laid on the table lets them use their final card.

In this case, the player may add the card to the meld and go out immediately, without drawing or discarding.

EXAMPLE

João holds only 2♠.

Maria lays down the run 3♠ 4♠ 5♠.

João may immediately add 2♠ to the run and go out, ending the round.

This play also has the highest priority over normal plays.

The opportunity applies to the meld that was just laid down. The player must go out immediately, before play continues.

Actions involving the most recent discard follow this order:

1. GOING OUT IMMEDIATELY

A player who can go out with the newly discarded card, without making another discard, has the highest priority.

2. PICKUP BY THE CURRENT PLAYER

If nobody can go out immediately, the next player has first choice to take the discarded card and may keep it in their hand.

3. PICKUP OUT OF TURN

The remaining players may take the card to lay down a valid meld immediately, following counterclockwise priority.

In addition, when a newly played meld lets another player go out with their final card, that player may do so immediately and interrupt the normal sequence of play.

Every valid go-out ends the round. No further draws or discards are made afterward.
At the end of each round, every player who did not go out receives points for the cards left in their hand.\n\nCards are scored as follows:

Cards already laid down on the table do not count.

EXAMPLE

A player ends the round holding:

5♠ Q♥ A♦

Their score is:

5 + 10 + 15 = 30 points

These points are added to the score they accumulated in previous rounds.

Every player begins the match with zero points.

At the end of each round, the value of the cards left in hand is added to each player’s total.

The player who went out receives no points for that round.

Scores carry over from one round to the next and are not reset during the match.

Players are not individually eliminated based on their score. Everyone continues playing until the match-ending condition is reached.

The match ends as soon as, at the end of a round, at least one player reaches 101 points or more.

At that point, every player’s score is compared.

The player with the lowest accumulated score wins.

EXAMPLE

The match ends because Pedro has passed 100 points.

João wins because he finished with the lowest score.

Reaching exactly 100 points does not end the match. The match ends only when a player reaches 101 points or more.
